title: Hamas deproscription
subtitle: Fahad Ansari, Riverway Law and the challenge to UK proscription
summary: The application to remove Hamas from the UK’s proscribed list: who brought it, the reported appeal history, the legal route and the documents still needed to establish progress.
jurisdiction: United Kingdom · proscription and POAC proceedings
scope: Legal-process reporting, not endorsement of Hamas or its violence. Hamas remains a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK. An application to change that status is not a decision changing it.
status_note: Checked 19 October 2026: the Home Office list still includes Hamas. A campaign update reports refusal in July 2025, an appeal in August 2025 and a 2026 procedural timetable. No final POAC determination or deproscription order has been located in this review; the timetable does not establish that its scheduled steps occurred.

sections.title: Start with the legal position
sections.intro: The application and the organisation’s current designation are separate facts.

entries.title: Hamas remains proscribed in the UK

paragraphs.text: Hamas remains on the Home Office’s list of proscribed terrorist organisations. The UK extended proscription to the whole organisation on 26 November 2021; its military wing had been proscribed since March 2001. Filing an application or appeal does not itself remove a group from that list.

Home Office guidance describes a written application under section 4 of the Terrorism Act 2000, normally to be determined within 90 days. Following refusal, the applicant may appeal to the Proscribed Organisations Appeals Commission (POAC), which applies judicial-review principles. A successful challenge and the steps implementing removal must be recorded separately.

sections.title: Fahad Ansari and Riverway Law
sections.intro: Identify the lawyers and their procedural role without equating legal representation with the client’s conduct.

paragraphs.text: Riverway Law’s press release identifies solicitor Fahad Ansari as its director and announces a section 4 application submitted that day on behalf of Mousa Abu Marzouk, a Hamas political-bureau official. It names instructed barristers Franck Magennis and Daniel Grütters. This establishes the team’s public account of the application, not acceptance of its arguments by a court.

The application argues that proscription conflicts with international-law obligations and disproportionately restricts speech, assembly and political discussion. These are the applicant’s legal arguments. The Home Office’s position remains that Hamas is a single organisation concerned in terrorism, rather than separable political and military entities.

entries.title: Why later sources use a different Riverway name

paragraphs.text: Legal Futures reported that Riverway Law ceased trading in its existing form on 29 June 2025 and announced a restructuring associated with Riverway to the Sea. This page retains “Riverway Law” for the original application and Fahad Ansari’s documented role; it does not infer a present solicitor-of-record or regulatory status from a later brand name.

sections.title: Progress and the limits of the public record
sections.intro: The following sequence is attributed to the deproscription campaign’s update. The underlying refusal letter and procedural orders have not been independently inspected for this page.

paragraphs.text: The Deproscribe campaign reports that the Home Secretary refused the Riverway application in July 2025 and that Hamas submitted seven appeal grounds to POAC in August. It also describes a separate CAGE application in June 2025. Those applications should not be conflated.

entries.title: January–March 2026 · further procedural steps reported
entries.kind: Campaign account, not an inspected order

paragraphs.text: The same update reports a January 2026 strike-out application by the Home Secretary involving closed material, followed by March directions concerning evidence. This is the campaign’s description; no conclusion about the merits or content of undisclosed material can be drawn from it.

entries.title: May–July 2026 · a timetable, not confirmation of compliance

paragraphs.text: The update lists 20 May for the Home Secretary’s reasons, 26 June for Hamas’s response, and 31 July for further government statements and evidence. Those dates have passed, but this review has not obtained the filings or a later determination. Scheduled dates are not evidence that documents were filed or that an appeal succeeded.

sections.title: What we need to establish next
sections.intro: Independent Tribunal research priorities: document the progress without manufacturing certainty.

entries.title: The next additions to the record

paragraphs.text: Seek the refusal decision, appeal number and filed grounds, public procedural orders, any open reasons concerning closed material, and the latest hearing notice or judgment. Record an event date, publication date, source type and outcome for each addition. A refusal, a procedural appeal and final removal from the list must remain distinct.

This page is a dated research starting point, not an automated monitoring service. It concerns a separate organisation and separate proceedings from Palestine Action’s proscription challenge. Findings in one case should not be transferred to the other.
